description: A two-student team from Irvine building a junior astronaut mission trainer. Interests: AI, coding, hardware, and space exploration.
summary: Mars Greenhouse Mission is a free science role-playing game that trains junior astronauts to keep a crew alive on Mars. Kids explore, learn, study, play and make. Players first live at a 3D Mars base for 20 sols, sharing limited solar power between oxygen, food, grow lights, heaters and radiation shielding. In Space Class, the base's scientists teach nine short lessons, each with a quiz and a badge. Then players take greenhouse missions from scientists and engineers, from easy to hard. Each mission runs on real weather measured by NASA's Curiosity rover and grows crops with NASA's real Space Station growing recipes. When plants die, kids read the charts, find out why, fix their settings and earn stars and ranks. The game runs in any web browser on phones, tablets and computers, with no download and no real names. It matters because future Mars crews will have to grow their own food, and kids learn best by trying, failing and trying again with real data.
details:
What it does

Mars Greenhouse Mission is a mission trainer built around five verbs. Explore a 3D Mars base, its greenhouses and real NASA discoveries. Learn in Space Class. Study like a scientist: run experiments on real Curiosity weather, read the charts and change one thing at a time. Play missions from easy to hard for stars and ranks. Make: a real automation system we built tests the game's watering rule on a real plant (see Earth test). The game has three parts.

1. The Mars base (3D). The player is the commander of a small base with two crewmates (made-up characters). Each game day is a real Curiosity sol, with that sol's real weather and a real rover photo. Every astronaut needs 0.816 kg of oxygen and 3,009 kcal of food a day, numbers from NASA's Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document. The player shares limited solar power between the oxygen machine, the greenhouses, radiation shielding and the night batteries. Solar flares and radiation storms come from NASA DONKI and Curiosity RAD data. The player walks between greenhouse domes (arrow keys or tap), uses each greenhouse console to learn what light, heat and water do, and chats with scientists on the paths for science badges. At a greenhouse door the game asks whether to go inside, then opens that greenhouse's controls, and a button jumps to the matching simulation mission. An off-road crew rover drives out of the base to seven sites, each showing a real NASA discovery with its source (for example the sulfur crystals Curiosity cracked open in 2024); where the sites sit on our map is made up. Goal: keep everyone alive for 20 sols. Easy, normal and hard modes.

2. The Mission Center. Players accept missions from a mission board. Missions unlock one after another:

  • Grow lettuce the NASA way (copy NASA's Space Station recipe).
  • The heater is off: see what a Mars night does to mizuna, then fix it.
  • Thirsty plants: the watering robot is set wrong.
  • The power puzzle: grow tomatoes with only 3 solar panels. Copying the full NASA recipe fails, so players must trade light against heat.
  • Dust storm wheat: keep wheat alive while dust blocks the sunlight.

Players set light hours, heater temperature, watering level, solar panels and dust. Each control explains what it does and what NASA used. The simulation then grows the crop through a full growing cycle on real Curiosity weather. A replay shows the rover's real photo for each sol next to a cartoon greenhouse where the plant grows or wilts, plus charts of temperature, soil moisture, power, light, growth and health, compared with the last try. A coach explains what went wrong on which real date ("on sol 4056 the room was only 5 °C because Curiosity measured -72 °C that night").

3. Space Class (Red Planet Classroom). Before or between missions, players go to class. Nine short lessons are taught by the base's scientists (made-up characters, and the page says they are not NASA employees): Mars weather, growing plants in space, solar power and dust, radiation, solar flares, what astronauts need, Curiosity's discoveries, thinking like a scientist (change one thing at a time), and talking to Earth. The talking-to-Earth lesson explains communication delay: why a radio message needs about 3 to 22 minutes to cross between Earth and Mars (today, November 15, 2026, about 11 minutes, from the real Earth-Mars distance), why even a "live" video from Mars would show the past, why a question and its answer take twice as long so the crew must act on its own in an emergency, and why NASA pauses commands for about two weeks during solar conjunction. Communication delay is taught in this lesson and in the base's space weather news; it is not yet a game mechanic of its own. Every number comes from the same NASA data the game uses, with the source under each lesson, for example Curiosity's real temperatures (-100 to 9 °C) and radiation doses. Each lesson ends with one quiz question and a badge, a "Read to me" button reads it aloud for young players, and finishing all nine gives a graduation certificate. Lessons point back to the game, for example the Curiosity lesson tells players to drive the rover out to see those discoveries.

Progress and safety. Players can sign in with a made-up call sign and a 4-digit PIN (no real names, no email). The best result of each mission is saved, stars give ranks from Space Cadet to Mars Commander, and a leaderboard shows call signs only. Without signing in, results stay in the browser.

How it works. A static web app (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Three.js for 3D) with a small server (JavaScript, runs on Node.js or Cloudflare Workers) and a SQLite database for players and scores. NASA data was downloaded and turned into small data files. The "Newest NASA data" mode downloads Curiosity's newest sols, photos and DONKI alerts when the game starts. Works on phones (touch) and computers.

What is real and what is a game estimate. Mars weather, sunrise and sunset, rover photos, radiation, flare alerts, crop growing recipes and astronaut needs are NASA data. How warm the greenhouse dome stays, how much power a panel makes and how healthy a plant is are simplified game numbers, and the game says so on screen.

Benefits. Kids learn that every choice on Mars costs power, that models are tested against data, and that failing is part of science. Teachers can use one mission per class period.

Earth test (Make). We verify the game's watering robot with a real automation system on a real plant. Our team built a small solar-powered watering box before the hackathon: an Arduino Nano ESP32 board, a soil moisture sensor, an air temperature and humidity sensor, a clock, a small pump, a solar panel and a battery. It waters a pepper plant with the same kind of rule players set in the "Thirsty plants" mission: the pump starts when the soil is below 35% and stops at 65%, with at most 2 minutes of pumping a day. When something looks wrong, its screen warns "CHECK TANK/SENSOR", and you have to read the data and fix it, just like in the game. The demo video and slides show only the device (photos and a short muted clip), with no people. The website's Board Panel (https://mars.shifu.studio/board.html) shows the box's live readings (read only), a short muted video of how the box and the pot are connected, and a diagram: the soil sensor tells the board how wet the soil is, the board flips a relay, the relay runs the pump, and the pump moves water from a bottle through a tube into the pot.

What we hope to achieve. More crops, missions and lessons, communication delay as part of the base game, a teacher mode for classrooms, and comparing the game's soil numbers with many days of readings from the watering box.

Tools. JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Three.js, Node.js, SQLite, Cloudflare (hosting tunnel). Demo video: screenshots of the game and Space Class, photos of the watering box, ffmpeg, an AI text-to-speech voice. Earth test: Arduino Nano ESP32 watering box (built before the hackathon).
